quests.conceptTitle: Pre-Reading Schema Activation: The Interpreter
quests.passage: Mr. Hara spoke for nearly a minute, calmly and courteously, and Amira, who had interpreted for the company for six years, translated it into a single sentence: "He says the timeline is difficult." The visiting directors nodded gravely. Across the table, Mr. Hara's colleague glanced at Amira, then at his notes, and said nothing. For a moment the only sound was the air conditioning, and Amira kept her eyes on her notebook. Later, in the corridor, he thanked her quietly. "You chose well," he said. "He was angrier than he sounded, and angrier than he should have been. If you had translated every word, we would have lost the contract." Amira shrugged. "I translate meaning," she said, "not just words. Though I'd prefer it if they didn't make me choose."

quests.conceptTitle: Pre-Reading Schema Activation: Where Did 10,000 Steps Come From?
quests.passage: The advice to walk 10,000 steps a day is so familiar that it seems to rest on solid medical research. In fact, it appears to have begun as a marketing slogan. In the 1960s, a Japanese company selling a pedometer called it the "ten-thousand-step meter", partly because the Japanese character for 10,000 resembles a person walking. The figure stuck. Later studies have examined the question more carefully. One large study of older women found that their death rates fell as daily steps rose from about 2,700 to around 7,500, and then leveled off. This does not make 10,000 a bad target; people who aim for it often walk more than those who do not. But it suggests the number is a convenient round figure rather than a scientific threshold.

quests.passage: Residents of Kingsway have every reason to be annoyed. For fourteen months the road has been a maze of barriers, shop owners report falling sales, and the opening date has slipped twice. Yet the complaints, however justified, should not obscure what the line will deliver. Cities that have built similar lines report that travel times on the corridor fell by a third, that car use dropped, and that property values near stops rose, which, admittedly, brings its own problems for renters. The council deserves criticism for poor communication about delays. It does not deserve criticism for the project itself. The sensible response to a difficult building site is to demand better management, not to wish the line had never been started.

quests.passage: Dear Sir or Madam, I am writing about the building site at 14 Fenner Street, which has disturbed residents of the adjacent flats since 2 September. The permit allows work between 8 a.m. and 6 p.m. on weekdays only. Nevertheless, on three occasions in the past two weeks, machinery began at 6:15 a.m., and on Saturday 21 September the site was operating at ten in the morning. I raised this directly with the site manager on 10 September, who assured me it would stop. It did not. I appreciate that construction creates noise and I do not object to work carried out within the permitted hours. What I object to is a pattern of breaches that the contractor has promised to correct and has not. I ask that the council investigate and confirm in writing what action will be taken.

FULL STOP." I wrote back, "Got it, Gran!" Her reply arrived four minutes later: "WHAT IS IT THAT YOU GOT? HAVE I BROKEN SOMETHING?" It took three weeks before she stopped signing off with her full name. Now she sends me photographs of her garden every morning, usually with no explanation, and I have learned to treat each one as a quiet good morning. Last Tuesday I sent her a photograph of my own breakfast. She replied with a single word: "Adequate."

quests.conceptTitle: Pre-Reading Schema Activation: Why Airlines Overbook
quests.passage: It seems absurd for an airline to sell more seats than a plane contains, yet the practice is common, and the economics are straightforward. On most routes, a few percent of passengers with tickets do not turn up, and an empty seat cannot be resold once the plane has left. Selling a small number of extra tickets lets airlines fill those seats and keep fares lower than they would otherwise be. The risk is that everyone arrives. When that happens, airlines first ask for volunteers to take a later flight in exchange for compensation, and the offer rises until someone accepts. Only if no one volunteers will passengers be bumped involuntarily, which regulations discourage by requiring higher payments. For travelers who are flexible, the system can even be an opportunity, though it is a nuisance for anyone with a connection to catch.

quests.conceptTitle: Pre-Reading Schema Activation: On Learning to Say No
quests.passage: For most of my twenties I treated every request as a test of character. A colleague needed help with a spreadsheet; a friend wanted company on a Saturday; a committee needed a volunteer. I said yes to all of it, and told myself that this was generosity. It took a quiet breakdown, in the middle of a task I'd agreed to without wanting to, to see that much of it was something else: a fear of being disliked, dressed up as kindness. Learning to decline has not made me less generous. It has made my yeses mean more, because people now know I would have said no if I'd wanted to. The strange part is that almost nobody has minded. The people who matter turned out to be far more interested in whether I was well than whether I was available.
